scope.scopeNotesMd: This report owns local changes to the R4 `RequestGroup` resource and its R6 successor candidate `RequestOrchestration`. The supplied R6 `StructureDefinition-RequestGroup.json` path is absent; the R6 package index contains `RequestOrchestration`, and `CodeSystem-fhir-old-types` lists `RequestGroup` as an old resource name no longer used in this FHIR version. Element-level findings therefore compare R4 `RequestGroup` with R6 `RequestOrchestration` after that identity mapping. Inherited-only changes from `Element`, `BackboneElement`, `Resource`, `DomainResource`, `BackboneType`, or `DataType` are excluded from `findings[]`.

narrativeReportMd:
# RequestGroup R4-to-R6 breaking-change assessment

## Bottom line
`RequestGroup` has a high-impact local breaking change: the R4 resource is no longer present under the same identity in the R6 ballot package and appears to have been replaced by `RequestOrchestration`. A raw R4 instance with `resourceType: "RequestGroup"` is not an R6 base resource instance. After applying that resource identity migration, several local element changes still matter: `reasonCode`/`reasonReference` merge into `reason` as `CodeableReference`, `action.participant` becomes a backbone actor model, and `relatedAction.actionId` is renamed to `targetId`.

## Scope
The analysis used local core package StructureDefinitions, package indexes, package metadata, and relevant local terminology artifacts. It excludes inherited-only base resource/datatype changes and excludes RequestGroup/SearchParameter/API behavior changes except as follow-up items.

## Main migration themes
Migration is not just a resource rename. Implementers need a structural transform that rewrites the resource type and canonical profile URLs, maps separated reason concepts/references into R6 `CodeableReference`, changes participants from direct references to `participant.actorReference`, renames related-action link keys, and establishes a policy for R6-only orchestration features such as action definitions, goals, input/output data-flow, locations, dynamic values, transforms, relative timing, and new status/intent codes.

## Highest-impact findings
The highest-impact findings are `RequestGroup:ARTIFACT_IDENTITY:root:8a6f3c`, `RequestGroup:ELEMENT_PRESENCE_OR_IDENTITY:reason:4f928d`, `RequestGroup:SERIALIZATION_OR_CODEGEN:action.participant:5dc0e1`, and `RequestGroup:ELEMENT_PRESENCE_OR_IDENTITY:relatedAction.actionId:3bf0af`. These cause direct R4-to-R6 validation or parser breaks for common instance shapes once the successor resource is used.

## Findings requiring human review
Human review is most important for confirming the official migration intent, deciding how much R6-only orchestration content must be preserved when down-converting to R4, and mapping new request status/intent values or broadened subject/participant targets where no local ConceptMap was available.

## Backward-compatible design observations
Some changes are expected for a renamed and more expressive workflow resource, but several could have been softened with deprecated aliases, retained old element names, or optional compatibility elements. The R6 model is richer and cleaner, but not wire-compatible with R4 RequestGroup.

## Follow-up analysis
Cross-artifact reports for base resources, CodeableReference, RelativeTime, RelatedArtifact, DataRequirement, and RequestOrchestration SearchParameters should be consulted before producing a production migration plan.

summary.executiveSummaryMd: `RequestGroup` is not present as an R6 resource and the likely successor is `RequestOrchestration`, making resource identity the dominant hard break. The top migration concerns are the resource/type rename, local action/reason structure rewrites, and R6-only orchestration semantics that cannot be represented in base R4. Confidence is high for computable StructureDefinition differences and medium for official rationale because no migration ConceptMap or narrative diff was supplied.
summary.migrationThemesMd: Treat migration as a resource transformation rather than a same-resource version bump. First rewrite `resourceType`, canonical profile references, and API/search surfaces to `RequestOrchestration`; then transform local element names and shapes: `reasonCode`/`reasonReference` to `reason`, direct `action.participant` references to participant actor backbones, and `relatedAction.actionId` to `targetId`. Down-conversion from R6 to R4 needs explicit loss/extension policies for broadened subject targets, definitions, goals, input/output links, location, dynamic values, relative timing, and new terminology codes.
summary.confidenceSummaryMd: Confidence is high for local structural, type, target, binding, and constraint changes because they are directly visible in the supplied package files. Confidence is medium for migration intent and exact official equivalence of `RequestGroup` to `RequestOrchestration` because the local R6 package lacks an official diff or ConceptMap; however, the missing R6 RequestGroup file, the R6 package index entry for `RequestOrchestration`, matching definitions, and `fhir-old-types` evidence make the successor identification strong.

findings.title: RequestGroup is absent in R6 and appears replaced by RequestOrchestration

oldState.summary: R4 defines a non-abstract resource named RequestGroup.
oldState.narrativeMd: The R4 core package contains `StructureDefinition-RequestGroup.json` with canonical URL `http://hl7.org/fhir/StructureDefinition/RequestGroup`, type `RequestGroup`, kind `resource`, and base `DomainResource`.

newState.summary: R6 ballot package has no RequestGroup StructureDefinition; RequestOrchestration is the likely successor.
newState.narrativeMd: The expected R6 `StructureDefinition-RequestGroup.json` file is absent. The R6 package index has `StructureDefinition-RequestOrchestration.json`, and `CodeSystem-fhir-old-types` lists `RequestGroup` as an old resource name no longer used in this FHIR version.

facts.note: The supplied expected R6 RequestGroup StructureDefinition path does not exist.
R6 fhir-old-types describes these as old resource names no longer used.

structuredDelta.matchingRationaleMd: `RequestOrchestration` has the same resource kind, same DomainResource base, a near-identical purpose statement, and carries forward RequestGroup action-orchestration structure with local changes. The R6 old-types code system explicitly marks `RequestGroup` as an old name.

impact.impactRationaleMd: This is a direct wire-format and type-system break. R4 JSON instances identify themselves with `resourceType: "RequestGroup"`; R6 base resources do not include that resource type, and the successor has a different canonical URL/type. R6 `RequestOrchestration` instances likewise are not R4 `RequestGroup` instances without an explicit cross-version transform.
impact.safetyOrBusinessRiskMd: Workflow orchestration resources often drive clinical/business actions; losing or misrouting them during migration can affect downstream decision support or order coordination.

justification.inferredGoal: Rename and mature the workflow orchestration resource model.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Retain `RequestGroup` as the R6 successor resource identity while updating definitions and content to the broader orchestration semantics.
justification.justificationRationaleMd: The inferred R6 goal is reasonable: the successor resource supports broader request orchestration and the `RequestOrchestration` name is clearer. However, the root resource identity rename is maximally disruptive for wire instances, REST routing, references, and generated APIs. The core semantic goal could largely have been met by keeping `RequestGroup` as the base R6 resource name and broadening its definition and elements, so this level of breakage appears probably avoidable.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: The strongest less-breaking base design would keep the `RequestGroup` resource type and canonical StructureDefinition as the R6 successor, update the description to the orchestration meaning, and apply child-element remodels separately. If HL7 wanted the clearer new name, a deprecated compatibility alias could reduce breakage, but that alias approach has a higher tradeoff because two canonical names for the same concept might persist.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: Preserves resourceType and canonical compatibility with the moderate cost of living with a less precise legacy name; an alias variant risks duplicate canonical names.

evidence.detail: R4 defines id/type/name `RequestGroup` at the RequestGroup canonical URL.
R6 defines the successor candidate as `RequestOrchestration` with a different canonical URL.
The R6 package index contains RequestOrchestration and no RequestGroup StructureDefinition entry.
R6 lists RequestGroup as an old resource name no longer used in this version of FHIR.

examples.examplesMd: The example is an illustrative minimal fragment showing the resource identity rewrite; complete validity also depends on referenced resources and profiles.

findings.narrativeMd: R6 does not continue the `RequestGroup` resource under the same name or canonical URL. Systems that deserialize by `resourceType`, generate classes from StructureDefinitions, enforce canonical profiles, or expose REST endpoints/search definitions by resource name will treat old R4 RequestGroup content as unknown until it is explicitly transformed to RequestOrchestration.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: An R4-valid instance with `resourceType: "RequestGroup"` is not valid against the R6 base package because the resource type is absent. Conversely, an R6 `RequestOrchestration` cannot be sent to an R4 endpoint as-is. This is independent of all child-element changes and must be handled first in migration pipelines.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Add an explicit resource-level migration step: rewrite `resourceType`, canonical profile URLs, type-specific routes, search parameter names, subscriptions, stored discriminator values, and generated class references from RequestGroup to RequestOrchestration. Then apply child-element transforms from the remaining findings. Regression tests should include parser dispatch, validation, persistence schema, REST endpoint names, and profile canonical references.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: The same domain goal could have been achieved with a deprecated alias or compatibility StructureDefinition, but the local R6 package did not include one. A major-version rename may be acceptable for specification clarity, but it is maximally disruptive for deployed wire formats and generated APIs.
findings.reviewerNotesMd: Although no official diff was available, the package evidence strongly supports treating RequestOrchestration as the successor rather than declaring the artifact simply deleted.

findings.title: reasonCode and reasonReference were merged into reason CodeableReference

oldState.summary: R4 used two separate 0..* elements for coded and referenced reasons.
oldState.narrativeMd: R4 instances represent reasons as `reasonCode` for concepts and `reasonReference` for references.

newState.summary: R6 uses a single 0..* `reason` element of type CodeableReference.
newState.narrativeMd: R6 unifies coded and referenced reasons under `reason`, with each repetition carrying a CodeableReference `concept` or `reference`.

structuredDelta.matchingRationaleMd: The R4 and R6 elements share cardinality, reference target set, and short text. The R6 CodeableReference shape directly subsumes the old concept/reference split.

impact.impactRationaleMd: After the resource rename, old R4 JSON properties `reasonCode` and `reasonReference` are not valid R6 element names. R6 `reason` repeats cannot be represented in base R4 without splitting each CodeableReference into one of the old arrays, and mixed or extension-heavy CodeableReference content may require manual policy.
impact.safetyOrBusinessRiskMd: Reason information can affect clinical/business justification and auditability; dropping it during migration can change interpretation of why a request orchestration exists.

justification.inferredGoal: Adopt CodeableReference to model a reason uniformly as either a concept or a reference.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Retain deprecated `reasonCode` and `reasonReference` while adding `reason` as `CodeableReference`, with rules to avoid conflicting duplicate reasons.
justification.justificationRationaleMd: The inferred goal is sound: `CodeableReference` is the R6 idiom for content that can be either a concept or a reference, and it removes the old parallel-field pattern. A less-breaking base design exists, but it is only partial because it would keep two ways to represent the same reason inside the same resource. Those duplicate representations could diverge and remain indefinitely, so the breaking unification is probably justified.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: A less-breaking base design would add `RequestOrchestration.reason` while retaining `reasonCode` and `reasonReference` as deprecated aliases for one major version. That would let R4 instances validate after the resource-level migration, but consumers would need rules for whether old and new reason fields may both appear, how to preserve element-level extensions, and which representation drives search and decision logic.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: Preserves old instances but creates parallel reason encodings and reconciliation burdens for ordering, extensions, search, and conflict handling.

evidence.detail: R4 has `reasonCode` 0..* CodeableConcept.
R4 has `reasonReference` 0..* Reference to Condition, Observation, DiagnosticReport, or DocumentReference.
R6 has `reason` 0..* CodeableReference to the same reference target set, with an example reason-code binding.

examples.examplesMd: The example shows a lossless straightforward mapping when each R4 repetition is purely a concept or a reference.

findings.narrativeMd: The reason model changed from two sibling arrays to one CodeableReference array. This affects validators, JSON paths, FHIRPath expressions, generated property names, search/extraction logic, and data-mapping code that previously handled coded and referenced reasons separately.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: Old `reasonCode` and `reasonReference` properties are unknown in R6 RequestOrchestration, so R4 instances using them become invalid after only the resource rename. R6 instances using `reason.concept` or `reason.reference` can generally be split back into R4, but the transform must preserve order/extensions where relevant and reject or extend any CodeableReference content that cannot be cleanly classified.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Map each R4 `reasonCode` repetition to `reason.concept` and each `reasonReference` repetition to `reason.reference`. Reverse transforms should split by populated CodeableReference child. Test concept-only, reference-only, mixed, repeated, and extension-bearing reasons. If order across old arrays matters to an implementation, preserve it with an extension because R4 had two independent arrays.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: A less breaking migration path would have retained the old fields as deprecated aliases. That would make validation and code generation more complex but would avoid rejecting existing R4 data. The current design prioritizes a single modern representation over wire compatibility.

findings.title: subject reference targets were widened beyond Patient and Group

oldState.summary: R4 subject targeted Patient or Group.
oldState.narrativeMd: R4 limited the request group subject to Patient or Group.

newState.summary: R6 subject targets ten resource types.
newState.narrativeMd: R6 permits CareTeam, Device, HealthcareService, Location, Organization, Practitioner, PractitionerRole, and RelatedPerson in addition to Patient and Group.

impact.impactRationaleMd: R4 Patient and Group subjects remain valid in R6, so this is not an R4-to-R6 instance break. The risk is down-conversion and generated code/business logic that assumed only patient/group subjects; valid R6 subject references to care teams, organizations, devices, locations, or providers cannot be represented in base R4 RequestGroup.subject.

justification.inferredGoal: Allow request orchestration to be about non-patient actors, services, organizations, devices, or locations.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Not applicable: R6 widens `subject` targets while retaining the R4 Patient and Group targets, so R4 subject values remain valid.
justification.justificationRationaleMd: Broadening the subject targets is consistent with a more general orchestration resource. Because no R4 target type was removed, this finding is not an old-valid/new-invalid base-design break for R4-to-R6 migration. The remaining risk is reverse representability or runtime handling of new R6 target types, not evidence that a less-breaking R6 base design was required.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: There is no applicable less-breaking R4-to-R6 base alternative to rate. Constraining the added targets in profiles or mapping them through extensions would be mitigation for systems that need R4 compatibility, but those are not backward-compatible base-design alternatives because the base R6 change already preserves R4 Patient and Group subjects.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: No less-breaking R4-to-R6 base design is needed; R6-to-R4 conversion and closed-model handling still need policy for added target types.

evidence.detail: R4 subject target profiles are Patient and Group.
R6 subject target profiles include CareTeam, Device, Group, HealthcareService, Location, Organization, Patient, Practitioner, PractitionerRole, and RelatedPerson.

examples.examplesMd: The subject value `Organization/acme` is valid by the R6 target list but outside the R4 Patient|Group target set.

findings.narrativeMd: R6 broadens the entity that a request orchestration can be about. This is useful for non-patient workflows but breaks assumptions in R4-era code that subject always resolves to Patient or Group.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: No old R4 subject target was removed, so R4-to-R6 validation is preserved for this element. Valid R6 instances using one of the added targets are not base-R4-representable and can fail R4 validation or generated model type checks.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: For R4-to-R6, no value transform is needed beyond the resource rename. For R6-to-R4, either reject non-Patient/Group subjects, map them through an extension, or define a business-specific surrogate such as a Group when semantically appropriate. Test all added target types if bidirectional conversion is required.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: The change is additive in R6 and therefore relatively safe for forward migration. The incompatible aspect is inherent to adding new base expressivity that R4 did not support; only an extension or profile convention could preserve it in R4.

findings.title: action.participant changed from direct Reference to participant backbone with actor[x]

oldState.summary: R4 participant was a repeating Reference.
oldState.narrativeMd: R4 encoded each participant directly as a Reference object in `action.participant`.

newState.summary: R6 participant is a BackboneElement with type, typeCanonical, typeReference, role, function, and actor[x].
newState.narrativeMd: R6 wraps participant details in a backbone. Actual actors are represented as `actorReference` or `actorCanonical`, and R6 adds participant type/role/function metadata and broader actor targets.

facts.note: R4 action-participant-type used patient, practitioner, related-person, device; R6 uses a richer set and changes related-person spelling to relatedperson.

impact.impactRationaleMd: An R4 participant item such as `{"reference":"Practitioner/1"}` has the wrong shape for R6, where the reference belongs under `participant.actorReference`. Generated clients also change from a Reference array to a backbone component array. R6 actor canonical values, metadata-only participants, and broadened targets cannot round-trip to base R4.
impact.safetyOrBusinessRiskMd: Incorrect participant migration can assign or display actions to the wrong performer or lose performer constraints.

justification.inferredGoal: Support richer participant constraints, roles, functions, actor definitions, and broader performer/resource types.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Retain the old direct `action.participant` Reference as a deprecated shortcut while adding a detailed participant backbone or distinct participant-detail element.
justification.justificationRationaleMd: The richer R6 participant model has a clear goal: it can describe participant type, role, function, and actual actor in ways the R4 direct Reference could not. A retained shortcut would reduce migration breakage for simple actors, but it would only be a partial alternative because it creates overlapping participant representations and leaves conflict and precedence rules to implementations. Those material tradeoffs make the breaking remodel probably justified.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: A less-breaking base design could keep the R4 `action.participant` Reference for simple cases and add a new backbone for detailed participant semantics, or allow a deprecated shortcut alongside the new backbone. This would preserve many old instances, but systems would need to reconcile shortcut references with detailed actors, and the deprecated representation could keep accumulating instead of converging on the richer R6 model.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: Preserves common direct actors but duplicates participant semantics and cannot represent type, role, function, or canonical-only participant constraints.

evidence.detail: R4 participant is 0..* Reference to Patient, Practitioner, PractitionerRole, RelatedPerson, or Device.
R6 participant is a 0..* BackboneElement.
R6 actor[x] carries the actual canonical or reference actor with many target profiles.
R6 action participant type codes are broader than the R4 set and use `relatedperson` rather than R4 `related-person`.

examples.examplesMd: The forward mapping for a simple R4 reference is straightforward, but R6-only metadata and target types need extension or loss policy when converting back to R4.

findings.narrativeMd: This is a substantial content-model change inside `action`. Existing R4 JSON paths, FHIRPath expressions, generated classes, serializers, and database mappings that treat `participant` as an array of Reference values need to be rewritten to handle a participant component with nested actor and metadata fields.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: A direct R4 `action.participant.reference` is not a valid R6 participant field after resource migration. Valid R6 participants may also lack an `actorReference` and describe a type/role/function constraint instead, or use canonical actors and target resource types R4 cannot carry. The break is both validation-level and runtime/codegen-level.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Map each R4 participant Reference to an R6 participant repetition with `actorReference`. If the referenced type is known, optionally set R6 `participant.type` using terminology-aware mapping, but be careful with `RelatedPerson` because the code spelling changed from `related-person` to `relatedperson`. For down-conversion, only actor references to R4-supported targets can be placed back into R4 `participant`; preserve roles/functions/canonical actors with extensions or flag for manual review.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: R6's richer participant model is understandable, but replacing rather than augmenting the direct Reference field makes existing instances and generated APIs break. A retained shortcut would have reduced migration cost but increased modeling redundancy.

findings.title: action.relatedAction.actionId was renamed to targetId

oldState.summary: R4 used mandatory `actionId` to identify the related action.
oldState.narrativeMd: Every R4 `relatedAction` had a required `actionId` element pointing to the related action.

newState.summary: R6 uses mandatory `targetId` for the same relationship slot.
newState.narrativeMd: R6 replaces `actionId` with `targetId`; cardinality and primitive type remain 1..1 id.

structuredDelta.matchingRationaleMd: The paths occupy the same parent position, have identical cardinality/type, and share the same short/definition role: identifying the action this relationship points to.

impact.impactRationaleMd: A R4 relatedAction with required `actionId` lacks the R6 required `targetId` and contains an unknown old element. The rename is easy to transform but hard for strict validators and generated serializers.

justification.inferredGoal: Clarify that the referenced action is the target of the relationship.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Keep the mandatory `actionId` wire name and clarify that it identifies the target related action.
justification.justificationRationaleMd: The inferred goal of making the relationship target clearer is reasonable, but the computable change is essentially a same-type, same-cardinality wire-name rename. R6 could have lived with the R4 `actionId` name and improved the short, definition, comments, and examples to state the target-action meaning. Because that alternative preserves old data with little long-term cost, the hard rename appears probably avoidable.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: A backward-compatible base design would leave `relatedAction.actionId` in place and update its definition to say it is the id of the target related action. If a `targetId` API alias was desired, it could be non-wire documentation or code-generation guidance. Adding both wire fields would introduce duplicate semantics, but simply retaining the old wire name avoids that duplication.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: Low tradeoff: the older name remains less explicit, but no duplicate field is needed and existing instances stay valid.

evidence.detail: R4 has required `actionId` 1..1 id.
R6 has required `targetId` 1..1 id.
The surrounding relationship element remains required and uses the same action-relationship-type code set, supporting a rename rather than a semantic replacement.

examples.examplesMd: The transform is a direct key rename for ordinary instances.

findings.narrativeMd: The related-action link key changed names while retaining the same mandatory id shape. This breaks strict JSON validation and code that navigates or indexes related actions by `actionId`.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: R4 instances with `relatedAction.actionId` become invalid in R6 because R6 requires `targetId`. R6 instances with `targetId` are invalid in R4. The migration is deterministic when no extensions depend on the old element id/name.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Rename `action.relatedAction.actionId` to `targetId` during forward migration and reverse the rename during down-conversion. Include tests for nested actions, multiple relatedAction repetitions, extension elements attached to the renamed primitive, and references to missing action ids.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: Because the primitive type, cardinality, and semantics are stable, this is the kind of break most amenable to a backward-compatible alias. The R6 choice favors clearer naming over preserving old wire compatibility.

findings.title: action.definition[x] was added and rqg-1 now allows exactly one of resource, action, or definition

oldState.summary: R4 action required exactly one of resource or child action.

constraints.human: Must have resource or action but not both

oldState.narrativeMd: An R4 action could point to a concrete resource or contain sub-actions, but not both and not neither.

newState.summary: R6 action requires exactly one of resource, child action, or definition[x].

constraints.human: Must have either resource, action, or definition

newState.narrativeMd: R6 adds `definitionCanonical`/`definitionUri` as a third mutually exclusive way to specify the action.

impact.impactRationaleMd: Existing R4 actions satisfying resource XOR child action still satisfy the R6 exactly-one rule. The break is representability in the other direction: an R6 action may be valid with only a definitionCanonical or definitionUri, and R4 has no equivalent local slot.

justification.inferredGoal: Allow a RequestOrchestration action to refer to an activity definition or definitional artifact without instantiating a request resource.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Not applicable: adding optional `definition[x]` and broadening `rqg-1` does not invalidate R4 actions that had exactly one of `resource` or nested `action`.
justification.justificationRationaleMd: The R6 goal of allowing an action to point directly to a reusable definition is reasonable. The updated invariant preserves the R4-valid cases because an action with exactly one of `resource` or child `action` still satisfies the R6 exactly-one rule. The incompatibility is for new R6 definition-only actions going back to R4, so ordinary extension or conversion strategies should not be counted as available base-design alternatives.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: Because this is an additive R6 capability rather than an R4-to-R6 validation break, there is no applicable less-breaking base alternative. Avoiding `definition[x]` would reduce R6 expressivity, while carrying it in R4 extensions would be a reverse-conversion mitigation rather than a different base R6 design.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: No less-breaking R4-to-R6 base design is needed; definition-only R6 actions still require R6-to-R4 mapping, extension, or loss policy.

evidence.detail: R4 rqg-1 required resource XOR action.
R6 rqg-1 requires exactly one of resource, action, or definition.
R6 adds definition[x] as canonical or uri with definitional target profiles.

examples.examplesMd: The R6 action is valid under rqg-1 because `definition[x]` is present and neither `resource` nor nested `action` is present; R4 would fail because there is no `definition[x]` element and no resource/action branch.

findings.narrativeMd: R6 expands what an action can be: it can now point to a definition rather than a specific request resource or nested action. That is useful for computable orchestration but creates R6 instances with no base R4 representation.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: Old R4 actions are not invalidated as long as they had exactly one of `resource` or nested `action`. Valid R6 definition-only actions are invalid in R4 and cannot be transformed losslessly without extension or materialization into a request/resource.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Forward migration does not need to populate `definition[x]`. Down-conversion should decide whether to reject definition-only actions, materialize a concrete request/resource, or preserve the definition in an extension. Test the rqg-1 invariant for all three branches and ensure transforms never create an action with multiple mutually exclusive branches.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: The exactly-one invariant is a reasonable update once `definition[x]` exists. R4 compatibility could only be approximated with extensions or by retaining no-op compatibility fields; neither would make base R4 systems semantically understand the new branch.

findings.title: R6 adds multiple root/action orchestration fields not present in R4 RequestGroup

oldState.summary: R4 had no root goal, action goal/linkId/input/output/location/applicabilityBehavior/endRelationship/transform/dynamicValue elements.
oldState.narrativeMd: The comparable R4 RequestGroup action model ended at priority/code/documentation/condition/relatedAction/timing/participant/type/behavior/resource/sub-action and did not include these additional orchestration metadata fields.

newState.summary: R6 adds root `goal` and several action-level orchestration/data-flow/customization elements.
newState.narrativeMd: R6 adds `goal` at the root and action level; `action.linkId`; `action.input` and `action.output` with XOR constraints between requirement and relatedData; `action.location` CodeableReference(Location); `applicabilityBehavior`; `relatedAction.endRelationship`; `transform`; and `dynamicValue`.

impact.impactRationaleMd: These are additive in R6, so they do not make existing R4 content invalid. They do, however, create substantial R6-to-R4 representability risk because base R4 RequestGroup has no local slots for goals, data-flow declarations, locations, transforms, dynamic values, applicability aggregation behavior, or end-relationship semantics.

justification.inferredGoal: Make request orchestration more expressive and align it with computable workflow/planning patterns.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Not applicable: the listed root and action elements are optional R6 additions and do not make R4 instances invalid.
justification.justificationRationaleMd: The added fields support richer orchestration links, goals, data requirements, locations, applicability behavior, transforms, and dynamic values. Since these are optional additions, they preserve R4-to-R6 validation for old content. The reported risk is that new R6 content cannot be represented in base R4, which is a reverse-compatibility concern rather than a reason to identify a less-breaking R6 base design.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: There is no applicable less-breaking R4-to-R6 base alternative for optional new elements. R4 extensions, constrained profiles that avoid the new fields, or lossy omission rules can help conversion to R4, but those are mitigations for round-trip compatibility and do not make `Yes` or `Partial` appropriate here.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: No less-breaking R4-to-R6 base design is needed; R6-to-R4 round-tripping may be lossy unless extensions or profiles preserve the new content.

evidence.detail: R6 adds root `goal` 0..* Reference(Goal).
R6 adds action input backbone with pld-0 XOR constraint.
R6 adds action output backbone with pld-1 XOR constraint.
R6 adds action location CodeableReference(Location).
R6 adds dynamicValue path/expression customization.

examples.examplesMd: The example uses several R6-only optional elements. R4 can keep the resource/action reference but has no base fields for the added orchestration details.

findings.narrativeMd: R6 RequestOrchestration captures more of the plan/execution context around each action. That is important for modern workflow systems but it means a down-converter must not silently drop fields that could determine applicability, data requirements, goal alignment, location, or dynamic value calculation.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: R4-to-R6 is safe for these additions because they are optional. R6-to-R4 is not safe: R4 validators reject the new element names, and generated R4 classes have no properties for them. If omitted, the converted R4 resource may remain syntactically valid but semantically incomplete.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: For R6-to-R4, define an explicit retention policy for each new field: extensions, companion PlanDefinition/ActivityDefinition references, out-of-band metadata, or rejection. Do not silently drop `input`, `output`, `dynamicValue`, `transform`, `goal`, or `applicabilityBehavior` in safety-sensitive workflows. Test the `pld-0` and `pld-1` invariants before conversion so invalid R6 data is not migrated.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: These are primarily additive R6 enhancements and are not avoidable if the base resource is meant to carry richer orchestration semantics. Backward compatibility is possible only through extensions or constrained profiles that avoid the new elements.

findings.title: action.timing[x] adds RelativeTime as a new choice type

oldState.summary: R4 timing choices were dateTime, Age, Period, Duration, Range, and Timing.
oldState.narrativeMd: R4 could express absolute, age-based, duration/range, period, or timing schedules, but not RelativeTime.

newState.summary: R6 retains the R4 choices and adds RelativeTime.
newState.narrativeMd: R6 adds `timingRelativeTime` for timing relative to another event or context.

impact.impactRationaleMd: No R4 timing choice was removed, so existing R4 data remains representable in R6. R6 instances using `timingRelativeTime` cannot be represented in base R4 without extension or conversion to an approximate Timing/Duration/Range, and codegen must add a new choice branch.

justification.inferredGoal: Support event-relative timing in orchestration actions.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Not applicable: `RelativeTime` is added as a new choice while all R4 timing choice types remain available.
justification.justificationRationaleMd: Adding `RelativeTime` is a reasonable way to express event-relative timing that the R4 choice set could not represent directly. Because the R4 timing choices are retained, old R4 instances are not invalidated. The incompatibility is for new R6 `RelativeTime` values flowing backward to R4, so extension or approximation strategies are conversion mitigations, not base-design alternatives.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: This finding is not an R4-to-R6 breaking base-design issue. Avoiding `RelativeTime` would limit R6 expressivity, while representing it in R4 with extensions or approximations would only address reverse conversion and would not be a less-breaking R6 base design.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: No less-breaking R4-to-R6 base design is needed; R6-to-R4 systems need policy for preserving or approximating RelativeTime.

evidence.detail: R4 timing choices are dateTime, Age, Period, Duration, Range, and Timing.
R6 timing choices include the R4 set plus RelativeTime.
RelativeTime expresses a time or period relative to an event and has its own constraints.

examples.examplesMd: The RelativeTime fragment is illustrative of the new choice branch; exact semantics depend on the RelativeTime datatype report.

findings.narrativeMd: R6 can now express timing relative to another event or definition. R4 clients generated from the old choice list will not know the `timingRelativeTime` JSON property and may drop or reject it.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: R4 instances using old timing choices remain valid after forward migration. R6 RelativeTime timing is not R4-representable in the base choice list and may require extension or approximation, which can alter scheduling semantics.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Update generated choice-handling code to include `RelativeTime`. For down-conversion, choose one of: reject RelativeTime, preserve it in an extension, or map only simple offset cases to an approximate R4 Duration/Range/Timing with documented semantic loss. Test relative timing with contextReference, contextDefinition, contextPath, and offset variants.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: Adding a new choice type is a standard way to add expressivity in FHIR. It is forward-compatible but not backward-representable; preserving compatibility would require avoiding the new datatype or using extensions instead.

findings.title: action.description and action.textEquivalent changed from string to markdown

oldState.narrativeMd: R4 modeled both text fields as plain strings.

newState.narrativeMd: R6 models the same fields as markdown, preserving cardinality and summary flag but changing the primitive type code.

facts.note: The wire primitive remains a JSON string even though the FHIR primitive type code changes.

impact.impactRationaleMd: The JSON scalar shape remains string-like, so ordinary R4 text values are unlikely to fail R6 validation solely due to lexical representation. The main risk is generated APIs and semantic/rendering behavior: `StringType` becomes `MarkdownType`, and systems may now render or sanitize markdown instead of treating the text as plain text.

justification.inferredGoal: Allow formatted markdown text for action descriptions and static equivalents.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Retain the R4 `string` type and update the definitions to say Markdown/CommonMark formatting is permitted and expected for these human-facing fields.
justification.justificationRationaleMd: The inferred goal of allowing formatted human-facing text is reasonable, and the JSON wire risk is low because markdown is still carried as a string value. However, changing the primitive type can break generated models, validators, and type-sensitive code. The same practical goal could have been met by retaining `string` and strengthening the definitions and rendering guidance, so the level of type-domain breakage is not clearly justified.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: A backward-compatible base design would keep `action.description` and `action.textEquivalent` as `string` while documenting that the content may contain Markdown/CommonMark and should be rendered or sanitized accordingly. That preserves R4 instances and generated primitive types. The tradeoff is that consumers lose the computable `markdown` datatype signal, so some renderers may treat the text as plain text unless they read the definitions.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: Preserves wire and generated-model compatibility with a moderate loss of computable type-level signaling for renderers and sanitizers.

evidence.detail: R4 description type is string.
R4 textEquivalent type is string.
R6 description type is markdown.
R6 textEquivalent type is markdown.

examples.examplesMd: No concrete old-valid/new-invalid JSON fragment was identified because both primitives serialize as JSON strings; the risk is mostly generated type and rendering behavior.

findings.narrativeMd: The element names and cardinalities stay the same, but the primitive type changes. This matters for code generators, validators that expose primitive subclasses, markdown sanitization, UI rendering, and tests asserting exact primitive type names.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: A typical R4 string value should still be acceptable as R6 markdown, so this is not classified as a hard instance break. R6 markdown content can be placed in an R4 string field as text, but R4 systems may render markdown syntax literally or fail to sanitize formatted content as expected.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Regenerate models and update code paths that typed these fields as plain string primitives. Review UI rendering and security sanitization for markdown. If down-converting, decide whether to keep markdown markup as plain text, strip formatting, or preserve rendering intent out of band.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: Changing the primitive type gives consumers a clearer signal that formatted text is intended. It could have been less disruptive by retaining `string` with narrative guidance, but that would lose useful type-level semantics.

findings.title: Required status and intent value sets add R6-only codes

oldState.summary: R4 status and intent use required R4 request-status and request-intent value sets.

terminologyComparison.terminologyNotesMd: Local complete CodeSystems were compared; terminology-server expansions were not run.

oldState.narrativeMd: R4 status codes are draft, active, on-hold, revoked, completed, entered-in-error, unknown. R4 intent codes are proposal, plan, directive, order, original-order, reflex-order, filler-order, instance-order, option.

newState.summary: R6 status and intent keep required bindings but add status `ended` and intent `solicit-offer`/`offer-response`.

terminologyComparison.terminologyNotesMd: The local R6 CodeSystems retain all R4 codes observed and add the listed codes.

newState.narrativeMd: The required bindings remain required, so new R6 codes are valid only in R6 and not base R4.

impact.impactRationaleMd: All observed R4 codes remain in the local R6 CodeSystems, so this is not an old-valid/new-invalid terminology break. However, status and intent are required modifier elements; valid R6 instances using `ended`, `solicit-offer`, or `offer-response` cannot be represented as base R4 RequestGroup without a mapping, and generated enum switches may fail on the new values.
impact.safetyOrBusinessRiskMd: Status and intent modify interpretation of workflow state and request semantics; an incorrect fallback can materially change workflow behavior.

justification.inferredGoal: Refine request lifecycle and negotiation semantics in R6.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Not applicable: the R6 required value sets add lifecycle and negotiation codes while retaining the R4 status and intent codes.
justification.justificationRationaleMd: Adding `ended`, `solicit-offer`, and `offer-response` expands workflow expressivity without making existing R4 status or intent codes invalid in R6. Because the change is additive from the R4-to-R6 validation perspective, the backward-compatible alternative question does not apply. ConceptMaps, enum fallbacks, or profile restrictions may be useful mitigations for reverse conversion and runtimes, but they are not less-breaking base R6 designs.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: There is no applicable less-breaking R4-to-R6 base alternative to rate. Avoiding the added codes would limit R6 workflow expressivity; mapping them to R4 approximations is necessary for R6-to-R4 exchange but may be lossy and belongs in conversion policy rather than this availability judgment.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: No less-breaking R4-to-R6 base design is needed; R6-to-R4 conversion and closed-enum runtime handling still need mappings for the added codes.

evidence.detail: R4 status binding is required to request-status|4.0.1.
R6 status binding is required to request-status|6.0.0-ballot4 and short text includes `ended`.
Local CodeSystem comparison found R6 adds `ended` and retains R4 status codes.
R4 intent binding is required to request-intent|4.0.1.
R6 intent binding is required to request-intent|6.0.0-ballot4 and short text includes `solicit-offer` and `offer-response`.
Local CodeSystem comparison found R6 adds `solicit-offer` and `offer-response` and retains R4 intent codes.

examples.examplesMd: Both new codes are illustrative. A production down-converter needs code-specific mapping policy rather than defaulting to `unknown` silently.

findings.narrativeMd: The required bindings for two modifier elements gained new codes. Even though existing R4 codes are retained, new R6 content can break R4 validators, generated enums, decision logic, and workflow state machines.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: Old R4 status/intent values remain valid in R6 based on local CodeSystem comparison. R6 instances using the added codes are invalid in R4 required bindings. Because the fields are required and modifier, a converter cannot simply omit them.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Update enums and switch statements for R6. For down-conversion, create an explicit ConceptMap/policy for `ended`, `solicit-offer`, and `offer-response`, with a documented fallback if no faithful R4 code exists. Test all status and intent values, especially modifier-sensitive workflow branches.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: Adding codes is the least disruptive terminology expansion for forward migration, but it still creates backward-representability risk. A formal cross-version ConceptMap would be the most useful compatibility mechanism.

findings.title: action.documentation gained a warning constraint limiting RelatedArtifact.type

oldState.summary: R4 had no RequestGroup-specific documentation type warning.
oldState.narrativeMd: R4 allowed any RelatedArtifact content permitted by the datatype and profiles.

newState.summary: R6 adds warning rqg-2 limiting documentation artifacts to documentation, justification, or citation.

constraints.human: RequestOrchestration related artifacts should only be documentation, justification, or citation

newState.narrativeMd: The new constraint is warning severity, not error severity, but it changes conformance expectations for the element.

impact.impactRationaleMd: The constraint is warning severity, so base validation should not reject old data solely for this rule. It is still a conformance risk for pipelines that elevate warnings to errors or use warnings for quality gates.

justification.inferredGoal: Clarify that RequestOrchestration action documentation should use informational RelatedArtifact types.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Not applicable: R6 uses warning severity for the documentation type constraint, so base validation does not reject R4 instances.
justification.justificationRationaleMd: The inferred goal of steering documentation artifacts toward documentation, justification, or citation types is reasonable. The base R6 design already uses warning severity rather than an error invariant, which is the compatibility-conscious choice. Any disruption comes from local tooling that treats warnings as failures, not from the base specification making old instances invalid.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: Because this is not a breaking R4-to-R6 base-design issue, a less-breaking alternative should not be rated as `Yes`. Replacing the warning with narrative-only guidance would be even softer, but the current warning is already non-fatal under standard validation and gives implementers a computable best-practice signal.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: No less-breaking R4-to-R6 base design is needed; local warning-as-error policies may still need operational adjustment.

evidence.detail: R4 documentation has only inherited element constraints, no RequestGroup-specific type warning.
R6 adds warning rqg-2 with expression limiting RelatedArtifact.type.

examples.examplesMd: An R4 instance using `RelatedArtifact.type` outside the listed set would receive an R6 warning rather than a base validation error.

findings.narrativeMd: R6 narrows the expected semantic use of action documentation. The element remains optional/repeating and uses the same RelatedArtifact datatype, but implementers should review values such as dependency/supporting-artifact types if they used this field for more than documentation, justification, or citation.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: This is not a hard instance break under standard validation because the new invariant is a warning. It can become operationally breaking where quality gates fail builds or imports on warnings.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Classify existing `action.documentation.type` values. Values outside documentation/justification/citation should either move to a more appropriate R6 field, be preserved with an extension, or be accepted with an explicit warning policy. Do not assume warning-free validation if old data used documentation for dependencies or related artifacts.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: Using warning severity rather than error severity is the backward-compatible design. The remaining risk comes from local operational policy rather than the base specification rejecting instances.

checkedNoMaterialChange.notesMd: For matched local elements other than added/removed/renamed structures, no minimum or maximum cardinality change was found. Mandatory local fields such as `status`, `intent`, `action.condition.kind`, `relatedAction.relationship`, and the related-action id slot remain mandatory.

No material target changes were found for `basedOn`, `replaces`, `encounter`, `author`, or `action.resource`; the material local target changes are reported for `subject`, `reason`, and `action.participant`.

Required bindings for request priority, action condition kind, action relationship type, grouping/selection/required/precheck/cardinality behavior retain the same local code sets based on local CodeSystem comparison, aside from version/status updates. Material status/intent additions are reported separately.
Local `status` and `intent` remain modifier elements in R6. No local RequestGroup/RequestOrchestration modifier flag change was found beyond inherited base elements that are out of scope.
No local summary flag changes were identified on matched RequestGroup/RequestOrchestration elements. Inherited summary flag differences, if any, belong to base-artifact reports.
No local fixed value, pattern value, or default value constraints were found to have changed materially for RequestGroup/RequestOrchestration.
No local slicing/discriminator changes were identified in the RequestGroup to RequestOrchestration comparison.

Root wording changed from a group to a set of related requests and many labels say request orchestration rather than request group. No additional hard semantic text break was identified beyond the identity rename and reported local element changes; rendered narrative pages and ballot notes were not reviewed.

nonBreakingNotableChanges.title: Successor artifact maturity/status increased
nonBreakingNotableChanges.whyNotBreakingMd: Changing the artifact status/maturity metadata from R4 draft/trial-use to R6 active/normative/FMM4 does not by itself invalidate instances.
nonBreakingNotableChanges.migrationAwarenessMd: The maturity change increases confidence that the R6 successor is intended for broader use, but it does not remove the need for explicit resource and element transforms.

nonBreakingNotableChanges.title: Example bindings were added to code and action.code
nonBreakingNotableChanges.whyNotBreakingMd: The new bindings are example strength and do not restrict validation the way required bindings do.
nonBreakingNotableChanges.migrationAwarenessMd: Terminology-aware systems may use the new examples for UI or analytics, but existing CodeableConcept values remain allowed by base validation.

nonBreakingNotableChanges.title: action.type extensible binding canonical moved to terminology.hl7.org
nonBreakingNotableChanges.whyNotBreakingMd: The binding remains extensible and the visible example codes remain create, update, remove, and fire-event; no local required-code removal was identified.
nonBreakingNotableChanges.migrationAwarenessMd: Regenerated terminology bindings may reference `http://terminology.hl7.org/ValueSet/action-type` instead of `http://hl7.org/fhir/ValueSet/action-type`. Terminology-server expansion would improve confidence for exact canonical equivalence.

nonBreakingNotableChanges.title: action relationship type code order/version changed but code set was retained
nonBreakingNotableChanges.whyNotBreakingMd: Local CodeSystem comparison found the same action-relationship-type codes in R4 and R6; the R6 StructureDefinition short text changes order and version only.
nonBreakingNotableChanges.migrationAwarenessMd: Do not treat the display/order change as a code removal. The new `endRelationship` element is covered as an R6-only addition.

followUpDependencies.reasonMd: Inherited base-artifact changes were intentionally excluded from local RequestGroup findings but can still affect validation, generated classes, and common fields such as language, contained resources, extension handling, and modifierExtension.
The local `reason` migration depends on CodeableReference semantics and any datatype-level breaking changes in R6.
R6 adds `action.timingRelativeTime`; datatype-level constraints and mappings determine whether any safe R4 approximation exists.
R6 action input/output and documentation constraints rely on these datatypes; their own R4-to-R6 changes should be reviewed before implementing conversion rules.
Required modifier code additions (`ended`, `solicit-offer`, `offer-response`) need an authoritative or locally approved mapping policy for down-conversion to R4.
The resource rename changes REST/search surfaces. SearchParameter differences were out of scope for this resource StructureDefinition report but are important for API migration.
